paper.title: CÆNL: Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning with Objective-Aligned Representation Control
paper.abstract:
Abstract Active learning changes the representations used to acquire subsequent
labels. We study this interaction through Collapse-Based Active Neural
Learning (CÆNL), which separates acquisition, Dynamic Collapse
Regularization (DCR), and its coefficient policy. DCR penalizes a
normalized within-class to between-class scatter residual above a frozen
reference, with a separate class-separation safeguard. Fixed, scheduled,
deterministic-feedback, and learned-feedback policies apply this objective.
The analysis establishes scatter invariances, conditional local descent,
and coefficient bounds, and shows why clean geometry alone cannot
guarantee input robustness. Six-seed classification comparisons are
complemented by a 104-run study with separate control selection and
ten-seed evaluations on each of two backbones. At 60% annotations on
ImageNet-100, entropy acquisition with DCR and MACC-Lite reaches 73.420 ± 0.512 % 73.420\pm 0.512\% accuracy on ResNet-50 and 73.086 ± 0.397 % 73.086\pm 0.397\% on ResNet-18 (mean ± \pm seed SD), exceeding entropy alone by 1.742 and
1.834 percentage points. Both gains survive Holm correction under
paired- t t and exact sign-flip tests, with unchanged feedback settings
across backbones. Independently tuned constants attain slightly higher
mean accuracy; the paired comparisons establish neither adaptive
superiority nor equivalence. Separate six-seed spectral studies yield a
small fixed-regularization C4 loss reduction, worse CIFAR-10 diffusion
FID, and inconclusive AudioCaps captioning effects. Earlier classification
studies find near-zero AutoAttack accuracy at L ∞ L_{\infty} radius 8 / 255 8/255 and no added benefit from learned control. The results support the
evaluated combined classification treatment and identify the task
dependence of geometry-informed regularization.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Active learning seeks to make effective use of a limited annotation budget by selecting examples from an unlabeled pool [ 1 ] . In deep learning, this selection depends on a representation that is itself updated after new labels are acquired. Uncertainty, coverage, and gradient diversity provide complementary criteria for choosing examples [ 2 , 3 ] , while the training objective determines how those examples reshape the representation. These two decisions interact: changing the learned features can alter subsequent predictions and acquisitions, even when the acquisition rule remains fixed. This interaction motivates studying representation regularization as an explicit part of the active-learning process. Neural collapse offers a geometric motivation for such regularization. During the terminal phase of classifier training, features from the same class become concentrated, and class means and classifier weights approach a structured configuration [ 4 ] . Relative within-class compactness and between-class separation therefore provide measurable properties of a developing representation. In an active-learning setting, however, the labeled sample and its class support change across rounds. A geometry measurement must be interpreted with respect to that changing sample, and a desired geometric structure must be connected to an objective that can influence training. The relevant question is whether using this information improves prediction at a given annotation budget. Turning geometry into a feedback signal introduces two design questions. First, the observed statistic should have an explicit relationship to the loss term whose influence the controller changes. Otherwise, a coefficient update may modulate an objective that does not directly penalize the measured deviation. Second, the benefit of the representation loss must be distinguished from the benefit of adapting its coefficient. Adaptive loss weighting has established precedents, including gradient balancing in multitask learning [ 5 ] ; here the feedback concerns a representation statistic within a task. A comparison with unregularized training assesses the complete treatment, whereas tuned constant and preset-schedule controls test whether observing geometry adds predictive value to coefficient selection. These considerations define our central question: under a common acquisition and optimization protocol, how does geometry-driven regularization affect prediction, and how do fixed, scheduled, and feedback-controlled strengths compare? We investigate this question through Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning (CÆNL), a framework with separately specified acquisition, representation-loss, and coefficient-control components. Dynamic Collapse Regularization (DCR) uses a normalized within-class to between-class scatter statistic for classification. A one-sided penalty acts on deviations above targets calibrated at initialization, and a separate safeguard discourages loss of between-class separation. The same statistic enters the loss and the feedback state, implementing objective–feedback alignment . The Meta-Adaptive Collapse Controller (MACC) provides deterministic bounded feedback in MACC-Lite and learned coefficient actions in Full MACC. Acquisition can use predicted-class geometric deviation or an established criterion such as entropy. This modular formulation allows the acquisition rule and the training treatment to be compared separately. Here, “collapse-based” refers to regulating relative class dispersion; the scatter statistic does not by itself characterize every property of neural collapse. The contributions are as follows: 1. Objective-aligned representation control. We formulate the normalized scatter objective, its fixed targets and separation safeguard, and the deterministic and learned coefficient updates within a budgeted active-learning loop. The formulation makes the measured quantity, the modulated loss, and the acquired-label information available to each component explicit. 2. Supporting geometric and control analysis. We characterize scatter decomposition and invariance, the local effect of an isolated regularizer step, and bounds on coefficient updates. An explicit full-update condition and a constructive robustness counterexample identify the additional assumptions needed to connect feature geometry to task behavior. 3. Controlled evaluation across methods and tasks. We compare acquisition rules and regularization controls in six-seed ImageNet-100 studies, followed by separate control selection and ten-seed confirmation and backbone transfer. Further six-seed studies evaluate spectral regularization for language modeling, image generation, and audio captioning, with task-specific outcomes and computational measurements. The principal classification finding is a benefit of the combined aligned-DCR and MACC-Lite treatment over entropy acquisition alone. At 60% annotations, the paired gains are 1.742 percentage points on ResNet-50 and 1.834 points on ResNet-18, and both survive the specified multiplicity correction. The feedback settings transfer unchanged between these backbones. The independently tuned constant has slightly higher mean accuracy in both cases, and neither paired comparison establishes superiority or equivalence. These comparisons distinguish the benefit of the complete classification treatment from the contribution of coefficient adaptation. The earlier acquisition and controller comparisons provide complementary evidence; their designs and statistical families are distinguished in Section 6.1 . The other tasks assess a separate spectral objective rather than the supervised class-scatter loss. Fixed spectral regularization produces a small C4 language-modeling loss reduction, all evaluated spectral conditions worsen CIFAR-10 diffusion FID relative to unregularized fine-tuning, and the AudioCaps comparisons establish no captioning benefit. Classification robustness is also evaluated separately, with near-zero accuracy under the specified AutoAttack threat model. These results make task performance the criterion for judging a geometric intervention and delineate the scope of the framework beyond its classification gains. Section 2 positions the approach in the literature. Sections 3 – 5 develop the formulation, controllers, and supporting analysis. Sections 6 and 7 present the protocols and results, followed by interpretation and limitations in Section 8 and conclusions in Section 9 .

sections.heading: 2 Background and related work
sections.text: CÆNL sits at the intersection of representation geometry, label acquisition, and adaptive optimization. These areas address different decisions: what structure features should acquire, which examples should be annotated, and how strongly an auxiliary objective should influence training. Reviewing these decisions separately helps identify the role of collapse-based feedback within an active-learning system.

sections.heading: 2.1 Neural collapse and its theoretical scope
sections.text: Papyan et al. [ 4 ] identified a coordinated terminal-training geometry: within-class variability contracts, centered class means approach a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF), classifier weights align with those means, and classification approaches a nearest-centroid rule. These properties jointly define the phenomenon. A scalar scatter ratio can measure relative class compactness, but cannot by itself verify ETF angles, classifier alignment, or agreement with nearest-centroid decisions. It is also distinct from the pseudoinverse-normalized NC1 statistic. We therefore use collapse as motivation for a measurable regularization target, rather than equating one favorable statistic with the full phenomenon. Theoretical work explains when such geometry is compatible with an optimization objective. Zhu et al. [ 6 ] analyze regularized cross-entropy in an unconstrained-feature model, where features are optimization variables rather than outputs constrained by a complete network. Under their assumptions, global minimizers have simplex-ETF structure and other critical points are strict saddles. This establishes a precise link between an objective and its optimal geometry, while leaving the feature-learning dynamics of a general finite network outside that model. Subsequent results show why architecture and regularization must be specified. Súkeník et al. [ 7 ] find regimes of the deep unconstrained-feature model in which lower-rank solutions are preferred to deep neural collapse. Their later work [ 8 ] establishes approximate collapse at global optima of particular regularized ResNet and transformer models with LayerNorm, with the approximation improving as depth increases. These results concern different models and assumptions. Hong and Ling [ 9 ] further analyze shallow ReLU networks with explicit data dependence: the conditions for collapse and its generalization consequences depend on architecture and signal-to-noise structure. Collapse can coexist with poor generalization in their low-signal regime. Recent work also broadens the geometry beyond a balanced simplex. Wang et al. [ 10 ] study feature–classifier space misalignment in long-tailed learning and introduce explicit alignment strategies. Alcala et al. [ 11 ] , in a 2026 preprint, characterize alternative configurations in the orthoplex regime, where feature dimension d d and class count C C satisfy d + 2 ≤ C ≤ 2 ​ d d+2\leq C\leq 2d . Together, these studies motivate measuring class separation as well as contraction. They also distinguish geometric alignment of features and classifiers from the objective–feedback alignment investigated here: consistency between the statistic penalized by a loss and the statistic observed by its coefficient controller.

sections.heading: 2.2 Discriminative and spectral representation objectives
sections.text: The use of within-class and between-class moments predates neural collapse. Fisher’s discriminant criterion [ 12 ] seeks directions that separate class means relative to within-class variation. DeepLDA [ 13 ] brings a discriminant objective into learned representations. Center loss [ 14 ] instead penalizes feature distances to learned class centers alongside softmax training. Supervised contrastive learning [ 15 ] uses class labels to bring same-class embeddings together while separating different-class embeddings. These approaches establish compactness and separation as useful, longstanding representation objectives; the use of class moments alone is not the contribution of CÆNL. The distinctions concern the quantity optimized and how it enters training. Center loss controls distances to learned prototypes, DeepLDA uses a discriminant criterion, and supervised contrastive learning operates through relations among embeddings. Our classification objective uses a normalized log ratio of equal-class-weighted scatter, penalizes only deviations above a frozen reference target, and includes a separate safeguard against loss of between-class separation. Its controller observes that same ratio. This construction permits direct comparisons between a constant coefficient, a predetermined schedule, and feedback without changing the underlying auxiliary objective. The present experiments evaluate those controls, rather than ranking all discriminative representation losses. Class-conditional contraction should also be distinguished from degenerate representation collapse. In self-supervised learning, VICReg [ 16 ] preserves per-dimension variability and reduces covariance redundancy while encouraging agreement between views. A useful representation can therefore require preserving variation, not simply suppressing it. This distinction is particularly relevant to our spectral extensions: reducing spectral complexity without class labels need not preserve the distinctions required for language prediction, generation, or captioning. Those extensions use a separate objective and require their own task evaluations.

sections.heading: 2.3 Active learning through uncertainty and coverage
sections.text: Pool-based active learning allocates annotations using the current model and the remaining unlabeled data [ 1 ] . Predictive entropy is an accessible uncertainty score, but uncertainty about an output and uncertainty about model parameters need not be the same. Gal et al. [ 17 ] integrate approximate Bayesian neural-network uncertainty into image acquisition, including Bayesian active learning by disagreement (BALD), which selects points for their information about model parameters. Such criteria motivate careful interpretation of any geometric score: distance from a class center is not automatically an estimate of epistemic uncertainty. Batch selection introduces a complementary coverage problem because individually uncertain points may be redundant. Core-set selection [ 2 ] addresses coverage in embedding space. BADGE [ 3 ] combines uncertainty and diversity by selecting from hallucinated last-layer gradient embeddings. Noise Stability [ 18 ] estimates uncertainty from output changes under parameter perturbations and relates the resulting selection to large, diverse gradients. These mechanisms use different information and incur different acquisition costs; an equal annotation count does not make their computational workloads identical. Uncertainty Herding [ 19 ] formulates uncertainty coverage to connect the low- and high-label-budget regimes. Its greedy selection balances uncertainty with coverage in a fixed feature space, addressing the budget dependence of purely uncertainty- or representation-driven selection. Our numerical comparison implements its margin-weighted coverage mechanism using shared-initial task-model features under the common candidate-pass and warm-start conventions specified in Section 6.6 . Recent acquisition methods make this balance adaptive. Jung et al. [ 20 ] study combinations of acquisition functions and their accuracy–computation trade-offs, including feedback-based aggregation. Cui et al. [ 21 ] use labeled-data feedback to construct a TrustSet and learn a batch acquisition policy. In CÆNL, the optional Mahalanobis score instead measures deviation from the predicted class using acquired-label statistics. It is a roundwise selection criterion. Our principal control study holds entropy acquisition fixed so that its comparisons address the training treatment; the acquisition alternatives are examined separately.

sections.heading: 2.4 Adaptive weighting and representation feedback
sections.text: Adapting the influence of loss terms is an established optimization idea. Kendall et al. [ 22 ] learn task weights through a likelihood formulation based on homoscedastic uncertainty. GradNorm [ 5 ] adjusts weights using gradient magnitudes and relative training rates to balance multitask learning. Both demonstrate that the choice of feedback signal is central to an adaptive weighting rule. Their task-balancing objectives differ from controlling a representation statistic within a single classification task, but they provide relevant precedents for learning or updating loss weights during training. MACC-Lite uses a bounded deterministic update driven by deviations of the monitored scatter statistic from its frozen target. Full MACC learns coefficient actions through a policy-gradient mechanism [ 23 ] ; its acquisition-policy head is disabled in the evaluated conditions. Thus the feedback acts on regularization strengths, whereas aggregation and TrustSet act on the selection of examples. Holding this distinction explicit avoids attributing a training improvement to a better query policy. This literature motivates a specific empirical question: once a representation objective is fixed, does observing its state improve the choice of its coefficient? A constant, a predetermined schedule, and feedback can produce different training trajectories even when they share the same loss. Comparing only against unregularized training cannot distinguish the usefulness of the loss from the usefulness of adaptation. Our separately tuned controls and subsequent confirmation therefore test that distinction directly. sections.heading: 2.5 Geometry, robustness, and predictive evaluation
sections.text: Representation geometry, predictive confidence, and resistance to input perturbations describe different properties. Su et al. [ 24 ] study neural collapse in both standard and adversarially trained networks, showing that small adversarial perturbations can disrupt the clean simplex structure of nonrobust models. Their analysis also identifies aligned clean and perturbed geometry in robust models. These findings make robustness a separate empirical question, rather than a consequence of clean-feature compactness. AutoAttack [ 25 ] provides an ensemble evaluation designed to reduce dependence on a single attack; its interpretation still requires the input norm, radius, and preprocessing to be stated. Calibration likewise concerns the relationship between reported confidence and correctness [ 26 ] . An auxiliary representation loss can change both accuracy and confidence, so we report calibration separately from the scatter statistic and clean accuracy. This evaluation perspective connects the literature to our experimental design: geometry motivates the intervention, while matched task outcomes assess its usefulness. The paper’s focus is the specified coupling of representation loss and coefficient feedback, with acquisition, robustness, and cross-task effects evaluated as distinct questions.

sections.heading: 3 Problem formulation and representation measurements
sections.text: The classification formulation distinguishes three roles for representation geometry: a differentiable training statistic, an aggregate feedback signal, and a sample-level acquisition score. The first two use the same normalized scatter measurement; acquisition uses a separate raw-feature distance. The spectral formulation for the other tasks is given in Section 4.5 .

sections.heading: 4 Objective-aligned DCR and regularization control
sections.text: Building on Section 3 , the classification method uses the normalized scatter statistic to define both a representation loss and the feedback that adjusts its strength. The construction has two time scales: coefficients act within training phases, while label acquisition occurs between phases. We first specify the shared objective and frozen reference targets, then the deterministic and learned controllers, and finally their integration into active learning. The spectral task variants use the separate formulation in Section 4.5 .

sections.heading: 4.5 Spectral formulation for language, diffusion, and audio
sections.text: The other tasks retain the idea of controlling a representation penalty, but use the covariance-spectrum formulation discussed in Section 2.2 . The penalty matches eigenvalue vectors rather than full covariance matrices. Smoothness is local to regions where the relevant eigenvalues remain separated. sections.heading: 6 Experimental design
sections.text: The evaluation follows the distinction between representation objectives and coefficient control developed in Sections 4 and 5 . Classification studies compare acquisition rules and regularization treatments at matched annotation budgets, then test feedback against independently selected constant and scheduled strengths. Separate language, diffusion, and audio studies evaluate the spectral variants under their task-specific protocols.

sections.heading: 6.1 Study organization
sections.text: Throughout this paper, a condition is a method configuration, a run is one condition under one seed, and a phase is one acquisition/training stage within a run. The initial ImageNet-100 comparison evaluated nine conditions across six paired seeds. After reviewing those results, we evaluated two additional conditions: entropy acquisition with aligned DCR and MACC-Lite, and a matched-protocol UHerding-Margin comparator. Each used the original six seed-specific initializations, targets, splits, annotation budgets, and evaluation endpoint. Their comparison lists were fixed before the additional runs, and their statistical families are reported separately. A third follow-up added entropy with fixed aligned DCR, retaining the same per-seed initial model and optimizer, splits, targets, floor penalty, acquisition protocol, and optimization schedule. Its two contrasts were declared before the new fixed-condition outcomes were inspected, after the entropy and Lite outcomes were already known. This later control adds six runs and 30 phases; it is not fresh-seed confirmation. The resulting classification record for these studies comprises 72 method–seed runs and 360 post-initialization phases across 12 conditions, with six paired seeds. A separate study then tunes fixed and preset-schedule controls on three new ResNet-50 seeds, confirms the selected comparisons on ten further ResNet-50 seeds, and transfers all settings to ten ResNet-18 seeds. Its 104 method runs, 23 shared initializations, and 520 post-initialization phases are additional experiments. The tuning, confirmation, and transfer seed sets are disjoint. They are not pooled with the earlier six-seed comparisons, and fresh seeds do not make the previously studied dataset an untouched benchmark. Engineering checks verify implementation behavior and are not counted as predictive-performance experiments. The original ImageNet-100 spectral pilot uses seeds 601 and 602. Saved-checkpoint attack diagnostics and a bounded aligned-objective development screen precede the final seeds 801–806. The aligned and spectral development protocols also differ in sampling, BatchNorm treatment, and integration choices; their absolute accuracies cannot isolate the effect of changing DCR. C4 uses six separate training seeds and an additional unused-shard evaluation of the same saved checkpoints. Diffusion development uses seeds 1001 and 1002, followed by confirmation seeds 1101–1106. Audio development uses seeds 1201 and 1202 for two epochs per condition; confirmation uses seeds 1301–1306 for ten epochs. Confirmation starts from the original pretrained assets and new seed-specific task components, not development-final checkpoints. Only audio confirmation evaluates caption-model predictions on the retained official test split. Development results are not pooled into confirmation inference.

sections.heading: 6.2 ImageNet-100 data and label accounting
sections.text: We use the fixed 100-class subset associated with Contrastive Multiview Coding [ 27 ] , drawn from ImageNet [ 28 ] . It contains 126,689 training images and 5,000 validation images, with 50 validation images per class. Original image bytes and dimensions are retained. A manifest records class mappings, source revision, paths, and SHA-256 values, which are checked before execution. The evaluated benchmark is ImageNet-100, not ImageNet-1K. Stratified sampling supplies 12,669 initial annotations per seed. The controller holdout contains 633 of these, leaving 12,036 gradient-training images. Five rounds each acquire 12,669 additional examples. Annotation totals are 12,669, 25,338, 38,007, 50,676, 63,345, and 76,014. The final gradient-training set contains 75,381 images. The final annotation fraction is approximately 60.0005 % 60.0005\% , reported as 60%. Holdout labels are included in every method’s annotation cost. Pool labels are consulted only after selection. The split procedure excludes holdout indices from gradient training and acquisition. A subsequent content-hash audit identifies five training–validation image matches and duplicate content within the training inventory. The frozen benchmark results are retained, with post-hoc duplicate-exclusion sensitivity reported in Section 7.3 . Index-disjoint partitions are therefore not asserted to be content-disjoint.

sections.text: The initial study and later confirmation use a randomly initialized ResNet-50 with a 100-class head; the transfer stage uses ResNet-18 [ 29 ] . sections.heading: 6.8.1 Language modeling on C4
sections.text: Pretrained GPT-2 [ 31 ] , with 124,439,808 parameters, is fine-tuned on a deterministic C4 subset [ 32 ] . Each of seeds 301–306 processes 99,999,744 tokens in 12,207 steps, with sequence length 1,024 and eight sequences per step. Baseline, fixed spectral DCR, spectral MACC-Lite, and spectral Full MACC share the budget and training configuration. The spectral implementation monitors h6 and h12 with target ranks 16 and 4, retained spectrum size 128, and a 2,048-token DCR subsample. Fixed strength is 0.01. Training uses the first English C4 training shard, with the first validation shard used for feedback and development (Appendix D ). All four conditions therefore evaluate the same single-shard training distribution. The original reporting set has 1,889 validation sequences, with 64 additional sequences reserved for controller feedback. After checkpoint selection and training were frozen, all 24 checkpoints were evaluated on validation shard 00002, which had not been used for local training, feedback, or configuration development. Each checkpoint makes 1,999,872 next-token predictions. NLL and accuracy are pooled over tokens; ECE is computed from pooled confidence-bin statistics. Perplexity is the exponential of NLL, not an independent endpoint. “Untouched” concerns local study use, not verified absence of GPT-2 pretraining overlap. Optimization uses learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 0.01, and 200 warm-up steps. AdamW has β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 ; one-dimensional, bias, and normalization parameters are exempt from decay. Norm-1 clipping and linear warm-up followed by cosine decay toward 10% of the base rate are used. Parameters remain FP32 with BF16 CUDA autocast. Spectral controllers operate every 25 steps. Both adaptive methods initialize their coefficients at 0.005 within [ 0 , 0.08 ] [0,0.08] . Spectral Lite uses step size 0.002 and deadband 0.1. Full MACC uses two 128-unit hidden layers, policy learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , exploration probability 0.15 0.15 decreasing to 0.02 0.02 , reward-baseline weight 0.1, and entropy coefficient 0.001. Its coefficient increments are { − 0.005 , − 0.0025 , 0 , 0.0025 , 0.005 } \{-0.005,-0.0025,0,0.0025,0.005\} . Its language-specific reward settings include validation-delta scale 5.0, value-delta clip 0.1, target-deviation weight 0.005, and zero query penalty. These settings are not replaced by the later diffusion/audio or aligned-classification controller settings. The unused-shard evaluator compares fixed DCR, Lite, and Full separately with baseline, giving three contrasts per endpoint. It reports individual paired- t t intervals and raw paired- t t and exact sign-flip values. sections.heading: Spectral sample axes and rank.
sections.text: The prefix representation reshapes eight embeddings per clip into 32 × 8 = 256 32\times 8=256 vectors of dimension 768. The pooled encoder representation has 32 vectors of dimension 768. Thus their centered sample-rank bounds are 255 and 31, respectively. The configured 64-entry spectrum is a storage and truncation dimension, not a claim of 64 nonzero eigenvalues for both representations. The encoder Gram spectrum is zero-padded to 64 entries as in Equation ( 17 ). A rank-16 template is feasible for both full training batches. The EMA-covariance monitor is distinct from either current-batch spectrum and can have a larger effective rank. Control operates every 50 steps and at the final step, yielding 278 adaptive events. The fixed coefficient is 0.01. Adaptive coefficients start at 0.01 within [ 0 , 0.05 ] [0,0.05] . Spectral Lite uses Equation ( 26 ) at both monitored layers, with step size 0.001, deadband 0.1, and target rank 16. Full retains the diffusion spectral-policy settings, replacing denoising feedback loss with caption loss on the audio holdout. Its terminal action is credited without an unused next action, and the acquisition head is disabled. The first 64 validation IDs in frozen manifest order provide controller feedback; the remaining 376 provide development assessment. Neither is used for task-model gradient updates. Final confirmation checkpoints evaluate all 866 retained test recordings. Beam size is three, decoding batch size is 32, and at most 30 new tokens are generated. The primary endpoint is CIDEr-D [ 42 ] from the retained pycocoevalcap /PTB path. BLEU-1–4 [ 43 ] , ROUGE-L [ 44 ] , METEOR [ 45 ] , SPICE [ 46 ] , SPIDEr [ 47 ] , and pooled token NLL are secondary outcomes. SPIDEr combines CIDEr-D and SPICE on their recorded scales. NLL is weighted by actual next-token target counts. A separate development diagnostic mismatches audio and captions deterministically without training updates. The three primary CIDEr-D contrasts compare fixed, Lite, and Full with baseline. Positive differences favor the regularized condition. Both paired- t t and all 64 sign flips are retained with separate Holm corrections across these three comparisons and individual unadjusted intervals. Secondary outcomes do not replace the primary endpoint. The six paired seeds remain the experimental units; repeated evaluation of 866 clips does not create extra training replications.

sections.heading: 6.9 Execution environment and reproducibility
sections.text: Experiments run sequentially on an IBM Cloud instance with one NVIDIA L40S GPU, PyTorch 2.6.0, torchvision 0.21.0, CUDA runtime 12.4, and Python 3.11.7. Seven of the 23 new seed holdouts contain one or two examples duplicated elsewhere in training; their counterpart enters the final gradient-training set in 24 method runs. None of the three tuning holdouts is affected. The exclusions by index operate as specified, but do not eliminate overlap by content. In a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, the same five validation indices are excluded for every method, retaining 4,995 examples. Lite-minus-entropy effects become 1.742 and 1.836 points on ResNet-50 and ResNet-18, while Lite-minus-fixed becomes − 0.188 -0.188 and − 0.328 -0.328 points. All six adjusted test decisions remain unchanged; excluding duplicate-content holdout items also leaves the selected controls unchanged. The planned 5,000-image outcomes remain primary. Evaluation-time exclusion does not undo possible training influence, and hash equality does not diagnose the source of the conflicting labels. Appendix B provides the sensitivity contrasts and seed-level endpoints.

sections.heading: 7.13 Computational cost and memory

Full MACC uses held-out task feedback in its state and reward and additionally optimizes a policy. These are training operations and can be omitted during ordinary logits-based classifier inference. Geometric acquisition between training rounds still requires feature extraction and fitted class statistics. Table 19 reports timing components for the initial nine-condition ImageNet-100 study. sections.heading: 8 Discussion and limitations
sections.text: The central question is whether representation geometry can guide regularization during active learning, and whether adapting its coefficient improves on a separately selected constant. The combined aligned-DCR and MACC-Lite treatment improves final-budget classification over entropy acquisition alone. The tuned constant attains slightly higher mean accuracy, with inconclusive paired differences. These findings support geometry-informed regularization under the evaluated protocol and motivate a separate assessment of the coefficient policy. Their interpretation connects the measured gains to the formulation in Sections 3 – 4 , the analysis in Section 5 , and the distinct task protocols.

sections.heading: 8.1 Implications for representation control
sections.text: The ten-seed comparisons provide the strongest evidence for the classification treatment. At 60% annotations, its gains over entropy are 1.742 percentage points on ResNet-50 and 1.834 points on ResNet-18; both survive the planned Holm corrections under paired- t t and exact tests. The feedback settings are unchanged across backbones, and the content-duplicate sensitivity analysis preserves the inferential decisions. Together with the earlier acquisition-rule ablation, these results show that the representation treatment can complement a standard uncertainty-based acquisition rule. The benefit does not require the proposed geometric acquisition score. The comparison with fixed strength addresses a more specific question. Earlier six-seed studies favor Lite over the prespecified coefficient 0.03 under adjusted paired- t t inference. In the later study, independent selection chooses 0.10, which yields slightly higher mean accuracy than Lite on both backbones. The Lite-minus-fixed effects are − 0.188 -0.188 and − 0.334 -0.334 percentage points, with individual 95% intervals [ − 0.529 , + 0.153 ] [-0.529,+0.153] and [ − 0.741 , + 0.073 ] [-0.741,+0.073] (Table 6 ). These intervals permit a disadvantage as well as a small advantage for Lite; they establish neither superiority nor equivalence. The earlier and later findings therefore concern different comparators. They support the importance of coefficient selection without demonstrating that feedback is the source of the gain over unregularized training. Lite exceeds the selected schedule under adjusted inference only on ResNet-18, further indicating that its relative performance depends on the control and architecture. The formulation contributes an explicit connection between the measured quantity and the intervention: the supervised scatter residual enters both the loss and the coefficient update. Section 5 characterizes this connection through an isolated local descent result and bounded coefficient responses. The recorded layer-dependent trajectories confirm that the implemented controller responds to the signal. These analytical and implementation properties make the mechanism interpretable, but do not establish that alignment is necessary for the predictive gain. The experiment does not independently identify the contributions of normalization, the separation safeguard, feedback, and the subsequently acquired examples. Moreover, a lower aggregate scatter ratio need not improve minimum class separation or control input sensitivity. The near-zero adversarial accuracy is consistent with this distinction between representation geometry and robustness. Full MACC adds learned actions but provides no established task benefit over the relevant controls. Its result is conditional on the specified state, reward, action space, and horizon; the present comparisons do not identify which of these choices limits performance. For practical evaluation, the tuned constant is therefore an essential reference alongside Lite. Both transfer here without backbone-specific retuning, so the transfer result alone cannot show that feedback saves tuning effort. The measured computation in Section 7.13 informs this comparison, but its protocol-specific timing boundaries do not support a universal overhead or deployment-efficiency claim. When representative labeled feedback data permit coefficient selection, tuned fixed DCR is the simplest regularized reference supported by these comparisons. MACC-Lite is an explicit feedback alternative, but the completed evidence does not establish a predictive or total-cost advantage that would justify recommending it generally. Full MACC incurs policy optimization without an established additional benefit under the tested configuration. Table 21 summarizes the findings and the scope of the corresponding inferences. sections.heading: 8.2 Limits of classification and statistical inference
sections.text: The classification evidence covers two ResNet backbones on one 100-class subset, with a class-balanced sampler and frozen post-initialization BatchNorm statistics. Matching these choices supports comparison within the protocol, but does not establish the best training recipe for every method. In particular, UHerding-Margin uses fixed shared-initial supervised features, capped candidate passes, holdout temperature calibration, and warm-start training. Its ranking cannot be generalized to uncertainty-weighted coverage methods under their original or independently optimized protocols. ImageNet-1K and ViT performance remain unevaluated. The endpoint also matters. Mixed early-budget ordering on ResNet-50 shows that a final-budget gain is not a uniform improvement throughout acquisition. No matched full-supervision comparison establishes an equal-performance annotation saving. Geometric atypicality may select unhelpful examples, while aggregate scatter can conceal a poorly separated class pair. Training anchors and all-class assessment differ in class support and transforms. Consequently, the measured geometry should be interpreted alongside predictive outcomes at each budget. New seeds quantify variability from initialization and data partitioning within this benchmark. They do not create an untouched image benchmark: official validation images were used for reporting during development. The five exact training–validation content matches with conflicting labels further prevent a claim of complete content separation. Excluding them at evaluation leaves the comparison decisions unchanged, but cannot undo their possible influence during training. The within-training duplicates and affected feedback holdouts reported in Section 7.3 also remain part of the study’s data provenance. Statistical interpretation must retain the distinction between study families. The original six-seed exact tests have the resolution limit derived in Section 6.7 ; their nonrejection does not independently demonstrate absent effects. The ten-seed family permits rejection and retains both test types. Paired- t t inference remains conditional on small-sample assumptions, and neither procedure provides study-wide error control across the full sequence of experiments. The later comparisons were specified before execution, but were informed by earlier findings. Keeping the original and later families separate preserves this chronology; it does not eliminate the influence of sequential development on the research questions selected.

sections.heading: 8.3 Task dependence and generalization
sections.text: The language, diffusion, and audio experiments evaluate spectral regularization, whereas classification uses a supervised class-scatter objective. Their joint value is to test the scope of geometry-based interventions across tasks, with outcomes judged by the relevant task metrics. They do not constitute a transfer test of one unchanged loss or controller across modalities. On C4, fixed spectral DCR produces a small loss reduction on an unused local validation shard. This is evidence for that objective and protocol, rather than for adaptive control. The result concerns a locally selected single-shard training subset and pretrained GPT-2; local non-use of the evaluation shard does not establish absence of pretraining overlap. In CIFAR-10 diffusion, every spectral condition worsens FID relative to matched unregularized fine-tuning. One possible explanation is that the imposed spectral target restricts variation needed by the denoising objective, but the present experiments do not test that mechanism. The result covers one pretrained U-Net, sampler, and training schedule, without determining whether a separately tuned spectral objective could behave differently. AudioCaps provides no established CIDEr-D benefit or statistical equivalence. Interpretation is limited by the approximately 89%-coverage third-party subset, possible AST pretraining overlap, and four flagged zero training clips retained under the frozen data policy. Exact identity and waveform checks do not establish acoustic authenticity or exclude all near-duplicates. These conditions limit comparability to the full original benchmark and extrapolation to other audio tasks. Across these studies, a geometric target is a modeling choice whose usefulness depends on its relationship to the task loss. The positive classification result, small fixed C4 effect, adverse diffusion result, and inconclusive audio contrasts motivate task-specific validation of that relationship. None supplies evidence of a universal cross-task gain, and the spectral outcomes cannot directly validate or invalidate the different aligned classification objective.

sections.heading: 8.4 Directions for further research
sections.text: The most direct next question is which component produces the classification benefit. A factorial comparison of the scatter penalty, separation safeguard, and coefficient policy, with matched control-selection budgets, would distinguish their contributions more clearly. Replaying common acquired sets across treatments would complement the current adaptive-acquisition experiment: it would test the training intervention conditional on a shared labeled sequence, while allowing sets to evolve would retain the full pipeline effect. These designs address different mechanisms and should be reported separately. The practical value of feedback also warrants a test beyond backbone transfer on the same subset. Predefined comparisons on new datasets, architectures, class-imbalance regimes, and annotation budgets could measure whether unchanged feedback settings reduce control-selection effort while maintaining predictive performance. Such a study should specify the primary endpoint and a meaningful effect size in advance, use a sample size appropriate to that question, and account for both tuning and training cost. Content-based grouping before partitioning, with label conflicts resolved or quarantined, would address the overlap limitations identified here. For the spectral variants, varying target rank and regularization strength would help test whether the observed task dependence reflects the imposed geometry or its magnitude. Any robustness extension would require an explicit link to input sensitivity or robust optimization, followed by a dedicated adversarial evaluation. These are directions for testing mechanisms and scope; their outcomes are not implied by the present clean-accuracy or representation measurements.

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.text: This study introduced CÆNL, an active-learning framework that connects representation measurements to an explicit regularization objective and its coefficient control. For classification, the same normalized within-class to between-class scatter residual enters the loss and feedback, alongside a safeguard against loss of class separation. Separating acquisition, regularization, and coefficient selection makes their roles open to controlled comparison. The supporting analysis characterizes the geometry measurements, conditional local regularizer descent, and bounded coefficient responses, while identifying the additional conditions needed to relate feature geometry to prediction and robustness. The full-update condition makes gradient interaction explicit, and the constructive counterexample shows that identical clean geometry and logits can coexist with arbitrarily small robust radii when input sensitivity is unconstrained. The principal empirical finding is a final-budget classification benefit from combining aligned DCR and deterministic MACC-Lite with entropy acquisition. At 60% annotations on ImageNet-100, ten-seed comparisons show gains of 1.742 percentage points on ResNet-50 and 1.834 points on ResNet-18 over entropy alone. Both survive the planned multiplicity corrections, with unchanged feedback settings across backbones. Independently tuned constants attain slightly higher mean accuracy; the paired comparisons establish neither superiority nor equivalence between Lite and those controls. The evidence therefore supports the complete classification treatment without attributing its benefit specifically to coefficient adaptation. The complementary experiments define the scope of this finding. Earlier acquisition comparisons show that the benefit can be obtained without geometric acquisition, whereas learned Full MACC adds no established classification advantage. Near-zero accuracy under the specified AutoAttack evaluation precludes a meaningful robustness claim. The separate spectral formulations yield a small fixed-DCR loss reduction on C4, worse CIFAR-10 diffusion FID, and no established AudioCaps captioning benefit. These task-dependent outcomes emphasize that a geometric objective must be assessed through the predictive or generative task it is intended to improve. The study provides a specified representation-control mechanism, conditional analytical guarantees, and controlled evidence for its use with entropy-based active learning. It also establishes tuned fixed regularization as a necessary empirical reference when assessing the additional value of feedback. Further work should isolate component effects and evaluate transfer across datasets and architectures under matched tuning budgets. The released implementations and numerical records support reproduction of the reported comparisons and further investigation of geometry-informed learning.

sections.heading: A.3 Development screen for the classification objective
sections.text: The aligned formulation was selected using a bounded development screen before the end-to-end classification comparisons. Each of two source seeds had a shared 200-step stabilization and five matched 2,000-step continuations on a fixed labeled set. The selection criterion required a favorable geometric direction and an assessment-loss increase no larger than 0.02 nats in either seed. This tolerance guided development; it was not a statistical noninferiority test. Relative to no regularization, spectral DCR changed the geometric-mean trace ratio by +0.077% and +0.054% in the two seeds. The corresponding changes were − 2.009 % -2.009\% and − 2.365 % -2.365\% for aligned fixed DCR, − 4.426 % -4.426\% and − 5.015 % -5.015\% for aligned Lite, and − 1.691 % -1.691\% and − 1.300 % -1.300\% for aligned Full. Loss changes were mixed but remained within the screen’s tolerance. These observations motivated testing the aligned objective under the full acquisition and training protocol; they do not themselves establish annotation efficiency or robustness. Final unused-shard evaluation uses en/c4-validation.00002-of-00008.json.gz . The latter shard was not used in local training or development; absence of GPT-2 pretraining overlap is not established. The CIFAR-10 diffusion study partitions the original training images for fine-tuning and internal assessment, while FID uses the complete original training distribution as its reference. The partition and official-test denoising assessment are specified in Section 6.8.2 ; the internal holdout is not claimed to be unseen during model pretraining. The coverage, exclusions, waveform checks, and possible AST pretraining overlap are documented in Section 6.8.3 . These data-specific conditions continue to apply when reproducing the reported comparisons.

sections.heading: D.2 Verification of saved results and execution records
sections.text: Verification of the initial classification study reconstructs metrics from saved validation, feedback, and attack arrays. Checks of the exported numerical records also reproduce paired effects and tests across classification, C4, diffusion, and audio, including the entropy-treatment budget curves and layer-geometry summaries. The server-recorded audio verification additionally recomputes caption metrics from saved predictions and original references. These checks establish the arithmetic of the retained records; they do not independently regenerate predictions, adversarial examples, generated images, or captions from raw inputs and checkpoints. For the control study, an independent NumPy/SciPy reconstruction checks all 104 final holdout arrays and 80 final official-validation arrays, including labels, logits, top-1/top-5 accuracy, cross-entropy, ECE, and class-scatter sufficient statistics. It also checks 543 training traces containing 4,155,880 recorded optimizer steps, 520 acquisition selections, and 40,872 control windows. Source and payload digests, split reconstruction, target calibration, learning-rate schedules, regularizer arithmetic, moving residuals, and applied coefficients are consistent with the recorded protocol. This reconstruction does not rerun checkpoint inference, recover individual feature vectors, or independently recompute every earlier-round prediction and acquisition-candidate score. Earlier-round learning curves use hash-verified summaries. The server exporter records verification of 543 checkpoint hashes; the checkpoint bytes were not included in the independent reconstruction. This distinction separates verification of saved evidence from a new execution of the experiment.

sections.heading: D.3 Audio model initialization
sections.text: Audio initialization required a bounded retry after a pre-training mismatch in the encoder positional parameter. A construction was accepted only when its whole-model digest matched the original seed-specific record. No training outcome or evaluation score entered that acceptance rule. The completed outputs, seeds, and acceptance records were preserved. The acceptance procedure enforces a match to the recorded model state, but does not resolve the underlying initialization nondeterminism. Accepted-state hashes alone cannot reconstruct their tensors, and the availability of all corresponding initial-state binaries is not established. Exact regeneration from seeds alone is therefore not claimed. This limitation concerns reconstruction of the initial state; it does not change the paired comparisons computed from the retained completed runs.

sections.heading: D.4 Released materials and access boundaries
sections.text: The repository identifies dataset revisions, source-file digests, experiment configurations, and exported per-seed measurements, together with the numerical reconstruction workflows. Raw licensed images, corpus text, audio recordings, and large model checkpoints are not redistributed. Original data-access conditions and the audio subset’s coverage and provenance limitations continue to apply. The release supports inspection and statistical reconstruction within the evidence boundaries described above; independent training or inference also requires the relevant data and model assets.

We study this interaction through Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning (CÆNL), which separates acquisition, Dynamic Collapse Regularization (DCR), and its coefficient policy. DCR penalizes a normalized within-class to between-class scatter residual above a frozen reference, with a separate class-separation safeguard. Fixed, scheduled, deterministic-feedback, and learned-feedback policies apply this objective. The analysis establishes scatter invariances, conditional local descent, and coefficient bounds, and shows why clean geometry alone cannot guarantee input robustness. Six-seed classification comparisons are complemented by a 104-run study with separate control selection and ten-seed evaluations on each of two backbones. At 60% annotations on ImageNet-100, entropy acquisition with DCR and MACC-Lite reaches 73.420 ± 0.512 % 73.420\pm 0.512\% accuracy on ResNet-50 and 73.086 ± 0.397 % 73.086\pm 0.397\% on ResNet-18 (mean ± \pm seed SD), exceeding entropy alone by 1.742 and 1.834 percentage points. Both gains survive Holm correction under paired- t t and exact sign-flip tests, with unchanged feedback settings across backbones. Independently tuned constants attain slightly higher mean accuracy; the paired comparisons establish neither adaptive superiority nor equivalence. Separate six-seed spectral studies yield a small fixed-regularization C4 loss reduction, worse CIFAR-10 diffusion FID, and inconclusive AudioCaps captioning effects. Earlier classification studies find near-zero AutoAttack accuracy at L ∞ L_{\infty} radius 8 / 255 8/255 and no added benefit from learned control. The results support the evaluated combined classification treatment and identify the task dependence of geometry-informed regularization. Keywords: neural collapse; active learning; representation geometry; feedback control; regularization; discriminative learning 1 Introduction Active learning seeks to make effective use of a limited annotation budget by selecting examples from an unlabeled pool [ 1 ] . In deep learning, this selection depends on a representation that is itself updated after new labels are acquired. Uncertainty, coverage, and gradient diversity provide complementary criteria for choosing examples [ 2 , 3 ] , while the training objective determines how those examples reshape the representation. These two decisions interact: changing the learned features can alter subsequent predictions and acquisitions, even when the acquisition rule remains fixed. This interaction motivates studying representation regularization as an explicit part of the active-learning process. Neural collapse offers a geometric motivation for such regularization. During the terminal phase of classifier training, features from the same class become concentrated, and class means and classifier weights approach a structured configuration [ 4 ] . Relative within-class compactness and between-class separation therefore provide measurable properties of a developing representation. In an active-learning setting, however, the labeled sample and its class support change across rounds. A geometry measurement must be interpreted with respect to that changing sample, and a desired geometric structure must be connected to an objective that can influence training. The relevant question is whether using this information improves prediction at a given annotation budget. Turning geometry into a feedback signal introduces two design questions. First, the observed statistic should have an explicit relationship to the loss term whose influence the controller changes. Otherwise, a coefficient update may modulate an objective that does not directly penalize the measured deviation. Second, the benefit of the representation loss must be distinguished from the benefit of adapting its coefficient. Adaptive loss weighting has established precedents, including gradient balancing in multitask learning [ 5 ] ; here the feedback concerns a representation statistic within a task. A comparison with unregularized training assesses the complete treatment, whereas tuned constant and preset-schedule controls test whether observing geometry adds predictive value to coefficient selection. These considerations define our central question: under a common acquisition and optimization protocol, how does geometry-driven regularization affect prediction, and how do fixed, scheduled, and feedback-controlled strengths compare? We investigate this question through Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning (CÆNL), a framework with separately specified acquisition, representation-loss, and coefficient-control components. Dynamic Collapse Regularization (DCR) uses a normalized within-class to between-class scatter statistic for classification. A one-sided penalty acts on deviations above targets calibrated at initialization, and a separate safeguard discourages loss of between-class separation. The same statistic enters the loss and the feedback state, implementing objective–feedback alignment . The Meta-Adaptive Collapse Controller (MACC) provides deterministic bounded feedback in MACC-Lite and learned coefficient actions in Full MACC. Acquisition can use predicted-class geometric deviation or an established criterion such as entropy. This modular formulation allows the acquisition rule and the training treatment to be compared separately. Here, “collapse-based” refers to regulating relative class dispersion; the scatter statistic does not by itself characterize every property of neural collapse. The contributions are as follows: 1. Objective-aligned representation control. We formulate the normalized scatter objective, its fixed targets and separation safeguard, and the deterministic and learned coefficient updates within a budgeted active-learning loop. The formulation makes the measured quantity, the modulated loss, and the acquired-label information available to each component explicit. 2. Supporting geometric and control analysis. We characterize scatter decomposition and invariance, the local effect of an isolated regularizer step, and bounds on coefficient updates. An explicit full-update condition and a constructive robustness counterexample identify the additional assumptions needed to connect feature geometry to task behavior. 3. Controlled evaluation across methods and tasks. We compare acquisition rules and regularization controls in six-seed ImageNet-100 studies, followed by separate control selection and ten-seed confirmation and backbone transfer. Further six-seed studies evaluate spectral regularization for language modeling, image generation, and audio captioning, with task-specific outcomes and computational measurements. The principal classification finding is a benefit of the combined aligned-DCR and MACC-Lite treatment over entropy acquisition alone. At 60% annotations, the paired gains are 1.742 percentage points on ResNet-50 and 1.834 points on ResNet-18, and both survive the specified multiplicity correction. The feedback settings transfer unchanged between these backbones. The independently tuned constant has slightly higher mean accuracy in both cases, and neither paired comparison establishes superiority or equivalence. These comparisons distinguish the benefit of the complete classification treatment from the contribution of coefficient adaptation. The earlier acquisition and controller comparisons provide complementary evidence; their designs and statistical families are distinguished in Section 6.1 . The other tasks assess a separate spectral objective rather than the supervised class-scatter loss. Fixed spectral regularization produces a small C4 language-modeling loss reduction, all evaluated spectral conditions worsen CIFAR-10 diffusion FID relative to unregularized fine-tuning, and the AudioCaps comparisons establish no captioning benefit. Classification robustness is also evaluated separately, with near-zero accuracy under the specified AutoAttack threat model. These results make task performance the criterion for judging a geometric intervention and delineate the scope of the framework beyond its classification gains. Section 2 positions the approach in the literature. Sections 3 – 5 develop the formulation, controllers, and supporting analysis. Sections 6 and 7 present the protocols and results, followed by interpretation and limitations in Section 8 and conclusions in Section 9 . 2 Background and related work CÆNL sits at the intersection of representation geometry, label acquisition, and adaptive optimization. These areas address different decisions: what structure features should acquire, which examples should be annotated, and how strongly an auxiliary objective should influence training. Reviewing these decisions separately helps identify the role of collapse-based feedback within an active-learning system. 2.1 Neural collapse and its theoretical scope Papyan et al. [ 4 ] identified a coordinated terminal-training geometry: within-class variability contracts, centered class means approach a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF), classifier weights align with those means, and classification approaches a nearest-centroid rule. These properties jointly define the phenomenon. A scalar scatter ratio can measure relative class compactness, but cannot by itself verify ETF angles, classifier alignment, or agreement with nearest-centroid decisions. It is also distinct from the pseudoinverse-normalized NC1 statistic. We therefore use collapse as motivation for a measurable regularization target, rather than equating one favorable statistic with the full phenomenon. Theoretical work explains when such geometry is compatible with an optimization objective. Zhu et al. [ 6 ] analyze regularized cross-entropy in an unconstrained-feature model, where features are optimization variables rather than outputs constrained by a complete network. Under their assumptions, global minimizers have simplex-ETF structure and other critical points are strict saddles. This establishes a precise link between an objective and its optimal geometry, while leaving the feature-learning dynamics of a general finite network outside that model. Subsequent results show why architecture and regularization must be specified. Súkeník et al. [ 7 ] find regimes of the deep unconstrained-feature model in which lower-rank solutions are preferred to deep neural collapse. Their later work [ 8 ] establishes approximate collapse at global optima of particular regularized ResNet and transformer models with LayerNorm, with the approximation improving as depth increases. These results concern different models and assumptions. Hong and Ling [ 9 ] further analyze shallow ReLU networks with explicit data dependence: the conditions for collapse and its generalization consequences depend on architecture and signal-to-noise structure. Collapse can coexist with poor generalization in their low-signal regime. Recent work also broadens the geometry beyond a balanced simplex. Wang et al. [ 10 ] study feature–classifier space misalignment in long-tailed learning and introduce explicit alignment strategies. Alcala et al. [ 11 ] , in a 2026 preprint, characterize alternative configurations in the orthoplex regime, where feature dimension d d and class count C C satisfy d + 2 ≤ C ≤ 2 ​ d d+2\leq C\leq 2d . Together, these studies motivate measuring class separation as well as contraction. They also distinguish geometric alignment of features and classifiers from the objective–feedback alignment investigated here: consistency between the statistic penalized by a loss and the statistic observed by its coefficient controller. 2.2 Discriminative and spectral representation objectives The use of within-class and between-class moments predates neural collapse. Fisher’s discriminant criterion [ 12 ] seeks directions that separate class means relative to within-class variation. DeepLDA [ 13 ] brings a discriminant objective into learned representations. Center loss [ 14 ] instead penalizes feature distances to learned class centers alongside softmax training. Supervised contrastive learning [ 15 ] uses class labels to bring same-class embeddings together while separating different-class embeddings. These approaches establish compactness and separation as useful, longstanding representation objectives; the use of class moments alone is not the contribution of CÆNL. The distinctions concern the quantity optimized and how it enters training. Center loss controls distances to learned prototypes, DeepLDA uses a discriminant criterion, and supervised contrastive learning operates through relations among embeddings. Our classification objective uses a normalized log ratio of equal-class-weighted scatter, penalizes only deviations above a frozen reference target, and includes a separate safeguard against loss of between-class separation. Its controller observes that same ratio. This construction permits direct comparisons between a constant coefficient, a predetermined schedule, and feedback without changing the underlying auxiliary objective. The present experiments evaluate those controls, rather than ranking all discriminative representation losses. Class-conditional contraction should also be distinguished from degenerate representation collapse. In self-supervised learning, VICReg [ 16 ] preserves per-dimension variability and reduces covariance redundancy while encouraging agreement between views. A useful representation can therefore require preserving variation, not simply suppressing it. This distinction is particularly relevant to our spectral extensions: reducing spectral complexity without class labels need not preserve the distinctions required for language prediction, generation, or captioning. Those extensions use a separate objective and require their own task evaluations. 2.3 Active learning through uncertainty and coverage Pool-based active learning allocates annotations using the current model and the remaining unlabeled data [ 1 ] . Predictive entropy is an accessible uncertainty score, but uncertainty about an output and uncertainty about model parameters need not be the same. Gal et al. [ 17 ] integrate approximate Bayesian neural-network uncertainty into image acquisition, including Bayesian active learning by disagreement (BALD), which selects points for their information about model parameters. Such criteria motivate careful interpretation of any geometric score: distance from a class center is not automatically an estimate of epistemic uncertainty. Batch selection introduces a complementary coverage problem because individually uncertain points may be redundant. Core-set selection [ 2 ] addresses coverage in embedding space. BADGE [ 3 ] combines uncertainty and diversity by selecting from hallucinated last-layer gradient embeddings. Noise Stability [ 18 ] estimates uncertainty from output changes under parameter perturbations and relates the resulting selection to large, diverse gradients. These mechanisms use different information and incur different acquisition costs; an equal annotation count does not make their computational workloads identical. Uncertainty Herding [ 19 ] formulates uncertainty coverage to connect the low- and high-label-budget regimes. Its greedy selection balances uncertainty with coverage in a fixed feature space, addressing the budget dependence of purely uncertainty- or representation-driven selection. Our numerical comparison implements its margin-weighted coverage mechanism using shared-initial task-model features under the common candidate-pass and warm-start conventions specified in Section 6.6 . Recent acquisition methods make this balance adaptive. Jung et al. [ 20 ] study combinations of acquisition functions and their accuracy–computation trade-offs, including feedback-based aggregation. Cui et al. [ 21 ] use labeled-data feedback to construct a TrustSet and learn a batch acquisition policy. In CÆNL, the optional Mahalanobis score instead measures deviation from the predicted class using acquired-label statistics. It is a roundwise selection criterion. Our principal control study holds entropy acquisition fixed so that its comparisons address the training treatment; the acquisition alternatives are examined separately. 2.4 Adaptive weighting and representation feedback Adapting the influence of loss terms is an established optimization idea. Kendall et al. [ 22 ] learn task weights through a likelihood formulation based on homoscedastic uncertainty. GradNorm [ 5 ] adjusts weights using gradient magnitudes and relative training rates to balance multitask learning. Both demonstrate that the choice of feedback signal is central to an adaptive weighting rule. Their task-balancing objectives differ from controlling a representation statistic within a single classification task, but they provide relevant precedents for learning or updating loss weights during training. MACC-Lite uses a bounded deterministic update driven by deviations of the monitored scatter statistic from its frozen target. Full MACC learns coefficient actions through a policy-gradient mechanism [ 23 ] ; its acquisition-policy head is disabled in the evaluated conditions. Thus the feedback acts on regularization strengths, whereas aggregation and TrustSet act on the selection of examples. Holding this distinction explicit avoids attributing a training improvement to a better query policy. This literature motivates a specific empirical question: once a representation objective is fixed, does observing its state improve the choice of its coefficient? A constant, a predetermined schedule, and feedback can produce different training trajectories even when they share the same loss. Comparing only against unregularized training cannot distinguish the usefulness of the loss from the usefulness of adaptation. Our separately tuned controls and subsequent confirmation therefore test that distinction directly. Table 1 summarizes the relevant methodological relationships and identifies the comparisons actually executed. Table 1: Positioning relative to representative acquisition, representation, and loss-weighting methods. Su et al. [ 24 ] study neural collapse in both standard and adversarially trained networks, showing that small adversarial perturbations can disrupt the clean simplex structure of nonrobust models.
